name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_1 - Force on charge due to positive charges

questiontext.text:
1.1 In Fig. 1.1, two positive charges \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) fixed along the \(y\) axis, exert a net electric force in the \(+x\) direction on a charge \(q_1\) fixed along the \(x\) axis. If a positive charge \(Q\) is added at \((x, 0)\), the force on \(q_1\)

Fig. 1.1

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two positive point charges \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) are fixed symmetrically along the \(y\)-axis. A charge \(q_1\) is fixed on the negative \(x\)-axis, and the net electrostatic force exerted on \(q_1\) by \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) is directed along the \(+x\)-axis. Subsequently, a positive charge \(Q\) is placed at \((x, 0)\) on the positive \(x\)-axis.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
We use the standard Cartesian coordinate system where forces directed to the right are along the \(+x\)-axis. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract along the line joining them.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges \(q_a\) and \(q_b\) separated by distance \(r\) is \(\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_a q_b}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\). By the principle of superposition, the net force on \(q_1\) is the vector sum of forces exerted by all other charges individually.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(q_2 > 0\) and \(q_3 > 0\) are placed symmetrically on the \(y\)-axis and \(q_1\) is on the negative \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-components of the forces on \(q_1\) cancel out. For the net force on \(q_1\) to be along the \(+x\)-axis (towards the origin), \(q_1\) must be attracted by the positive charges \(q_2\) and \(q_3\), which means \(q_1\) is negative (\(q_1 < 0\)).
When the positive charge \(Q\) is placed at \((x, 0)\) on the positive \(x\)-axis, \(Q\) exerts an attractive force on the negative charge \(q_1\). Since \(Q\) lies to the right of \(q_1\), this additional attractive force is also directed along the \(+x\)-axis.
Note that the presence of \(Q\) does not alter the individual forces exerted by \(q_2\) and \(q_3\) on \(q_1\) (superposition principle).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Adding a force in the \(+x\) direction to an existing net force in the \(+x\) direction increases the magnitude of the net force in the same direction. Therefore, the force on \(q_1\) shall increase along the positive \(x\)-axis.

answer.text: shall increase along the positive \(x\)-axis.
shall decrease along the positive \(x\)-axis.
shall point along the negative \(x\)-axis.
shall increase but the direction changes because of the intersection of \(Q\) with \(q_2\) and \(q_3\).

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_2 - Electric field of point charge near conducting sphere

questiontext.text:
1.2 A point positive charge is brought near an isolated conducting sphere (Fig. 1.2). The electric field is best given by

(i)

(ii)

(iii)

Fig. 1.2

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero, and electric field lines always meet or leave the surface of a conductor perpendicularly (at \(90^\circ\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
When a positive point charge \(+q\) is brought near an isolated conducting sphere, electrostatic induction causes negative charges to accumulate on the near side of the sphere and an equal amount of positive charge to accumulate on the far side of the sphere.

Step 3: Application
Electric field lines originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges. Thus, field lines start from \(+q\) and terminate perpendicularly on the negatively charged near surface of the sphere. From the positively charged far surface, field lines originate perpendicularly and extend outward. Inside the sphere, there are no electric field lines.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct electric field configuration is the one where field lines originate from \(+q\), curve to strike the near surface of the sphere perpendicularly, are absent inside the sphere, and emerge perpendicularly outward from the far surface of the sphere, which corresponds to Fig (i).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four closed Gaussian surfaces \(S\) of different shapes and sizes are shown, each enclosing a single point charge \(+q\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each surface \(S\) is a closed surface in three-dimensional space, and the outward normal is taken as positive for electric flux.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Gauss's law, the total electric flux \(\Phi_E\) through any closed surface \(S\) is given by \(\Phi_E = \oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\), where \(q_{\text{enc}}\) is the net charge enclosed by the surface.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In all four cases, the net charge enclosed inside the closed surface \(S\) is \(+q\). Since Gauss's law depends only on the net enclosed charge and is independent of the shape, size of the closed surface, or the position of the charge within it, the electric flux is \(\Phi_E = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\) for every surface.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because the enclosed charge is identical in every case, the electric flux is the same for all the figures.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_4 - Contributions to electric field and charge in Gauss law

questiontext.text:
1.4 Five charges \(q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4\), and \(q_5\) are fixed at their positions as shown in Fig. 1.4. \(S\) is a Gaussian surface. The Gauss's law is given by

\[\oint_{S} \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{s} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\]

Which of the following statements is correct?

Fig. 1.4

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Five point charges \(q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4\), and \(q_5\) are fixed in space. From the diagram, charges \(q_2\) and \(q_4\) lie inside the closed Gaussian surface \(S\), while charges \(q_1, q_3\), and \(q_5\) lie outside \(S\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The surface \(S\) is a closed Gaussian surface, and the electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) on \(S\) is the resultant electric field at each surface element.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Gauss's law states that \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{s} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\), where \(\mathbf{E}\) is the net electric field at any point on the Gaussian surface due to all charges present in space (both inside and outside \(S\)), and \(q\) is the net charge enclosed inside \(S\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Every charge in the system (\(q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4\), and \(q_5\)) produces an electric field at points on the surface \(S\), so \(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS has a contribution from all charges. However, the net flux due to any charge outside \(S\) (\(q_1, q_3, q_5\)) is zero, so the RHS depends only on the enclosed charges \(q_2\) and \(q_4\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, \(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS has a contribution from all charges while \(q\) on the RHS has a contribution from \(q_2\) and \(q_4\) only.

answer.text: \(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS of the above equation will have a contribution from \(q_1, q_5\) and \(q_3\) while \(q\) on the RHS will have a contribution from \(q_2\) and \(q_4\) only.
\(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS of the above equation will have a contribution from all charges while \(q\) on the RHS will have a contribution from \(q_2\) and \(q_4\) only.
\(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS of the above equation will have a contribution from all charges while \(q\) on the RHS will have a contribution from \(q_1, q_3\) and \(q_5\) only.
Both \(\mathbf{E}\) on the LHS and \(q\) on the RHS will have contributions from \(q_2\) and \(q_4\) only.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_5 - Force on electric dipole in non-uniform field

questiontext.text:
1.5 Figure 1.5 shows electric field lines in which an electric dipole \(\mathbf{p}\) is placed as shown. Which of the following statements is correct?

Fig. 1.5

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An electric dipole \(\mathbf{p}\) consists of \(-q\) on the left and \(+q\) on the right, placed in an electric field whose field lines diverge towards the right.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The density of electric field lines represents the magnitude of the electric field \(\mathbf{E}\). Closer lines indicate a stronger electric field, and wider spacing indicates a weaker electric field.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electrostatic force on a charge \(q\) in an electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) is \(\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{E}\). A positive charge experiences a force in the direction of \(\mathbf{E}\), while a negative charge experiences a force opposite to \(\mathbf{E}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because the field lines diverge towards the right, the electric field is stronger at the position of \(-q\) (left) than at the position of \(+q\) (right), i.e., \(E_{-q} > E_{+q}\).
The force on \(+q\) is \(F_{+q} = qE_{+q}\) towards the right, and the force on \(-q\) is \(F_{-q} = qE_{-q}\) towards the left.
Since \(E_{-q} > E_{+q}\), we have \(F_{-q} > F_{+q}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The leftward force on \(-q\) exceeds the rightward force on \(+q\), so the dipole will experience a net force towards the left.

answer.text: The dipole will not experience any force.
The dipole will experience a force towards right.
The dipole will experience a force towards left.
The dipole will experience a force upwards.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_6 - Electric field on other side of conducting plane

questiontext.text: 1.6 A point charge \(+q\), is placed at a distance \(d\) from an isolated conducting plane. The field at a point P on the other side of the plane is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When a point charge is placed near an isolated conducting plane, electrostatic induction redistributes the free charges on the conductor's surfaces such that the electric field inside the conductor is zero and the surface of the conductor is an equipotential.

Step 2: Evaluation
A positive point charge \(+q\) at distance \(d\) on one side induces a negative charge on the face of the conducting plane nearest to \(+q\). Since the conducting plane is isolated (electrically neutral overall), an equal positive charge is induced on the opposite face of the plane.

Step 3: Application
Because the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential surface, the electric field lines just outside the opposite face must be perpendicular to the plane. Since this opposite face carries induced positive charge, the electric field lines are directed away from the plane.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the electric field at a point P on the other side of the plane is directed perpendicular to the plane and away from the plane.

answer.text: directed perpendicular to the plane and away from the plane.
directed perpendicular to the plane but towards the plane.
directed radially away from the point charge.
directed radially towards the point charge.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQI_Q1_7 - Electric field of uniformly charged hemisphere on diameter

questiontext.text: 1.7 A hemisphere is uniformly charged positively. The electric field at a point on a diameter away from the centre is directed

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electric field inside a uniformly charged spherical shell is zero everywhere. By the principle of superposition, a full spherical shell can be viewed as the combination of an upper hemisphere and a symmetric lower hemisphere.

Step 2: Evaluation
Consider a point on a diameter in the equatorial plane of the uniformly positively charged hemispherical shell, away from the centre. By symmetry about the equatorial plane, any charge element on the upper hemisphere has a mirror-image counterpart on the lower hemisphere with the same component of electric field parallel to the diameter.

Step 3: Application
Since the net electric field inside a complete uniformly charged spherical shell is zero, the sum of the parallel components from the upper and lower hemispheres must be zero. As these two parallel components are equal, each must individually be zero. Thus, the electric field at any point on the diameter has no component along the diameter. Furthermore, since all positive charges of the hemisphere lie on one side of the equatorial plane, the net electric field points away from that side, perpendicular to the diameter.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Hence, the electric field at a point on a diameter away from the centre is directed perpendicular to the diameter.

answer.text: perpendicular to the diameter
parallel to the diameter
at an angle tilted towards the diameter
at an angle tilted away from the diameter.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_8 - Zero electric flux over a closed surface

questiontext.text: 1.8 If \(\oint_s \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\) over a surface, then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Gauss's law, the net electric flux through a closed surface \(S\) is \(\Phi_E = \oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\), where \(q_{\text{enc}}\) is the net charge enclosed by the surface.

Step 2: Evaluation
If \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\), it implies that the net electric flux through the closed surface is zero, meaning the total number of electric field lines entering the surface equals the total number of electric field lines leaving it.

Step 3: Application
Zero net flux does not require the electric field inside or on the surface to be zero or uniform (for instance, a charge outside the surface produces a non-uniform, non-zero field on and inside the surface with zero net flux). Similarly, it does not require all charges to be outside the surface, because equal and opposite charges (such as an electric dipole) can be enclosed inside, yielding \(q_{\text{enc}} = 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the only necessarily true statement is that the number of flux lines entering the surface must be equal to the number of flux lines leaving it.

answer.text: the electric field inside the surface and on it is zero.
the electric field inside the surface is necessarily uniform.
the number of flux lines entering the surface must be equal to the number of flux lines leaving it.
all charges must necessarily be outside the surface.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_9 - Continuity of electric field at a point

questiontext.text: 1.9 The Electric field at a point is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electric field due to a charge distribution is governed by Coulomb's law and Gauss's law. In charge-free space, the electric field varies smoothly with position.

Step 2: Evaluation
If there is no charge at a given point, there is no source or sink of electric field lines at that point, so the electric field is continuous there. Conversely, if a charge (positive or negative) is present at a point, the electric field experiences a discontinuity (or diverges to infinity for a point charge, or jumps across a charged surface by \(\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the electric field at a point is continuous if there is no charge at that point, and discontinuous if there is a charge at that point.

answer.text: always continuous.
continuous if there is no charge at that point.
discontinuous only if there is a negative charge at that point.
discontinuous if there is a charge at that point.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_10 - Gauss law with only one type of charge

questiontext.text: 1.10 If there were only one type of charge in the universe, then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gauss's law states that the electric flux through any closed surface \(S\) is \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\), which depends on the inverse-square nature of Coulomb's law and remains valid regardless of whether one or both types of charges exist.

Step 2: Evaluation
If only one type of charge existed, any closed surface enclosing no charge (i.e., when the charge is outside the surface) would still have zero net flux: \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\), because every field line entering the surface also leaves it. Furthermore, if charges of magnitude \(q\) are enclosed inside the surface, the flux through the surface is still defined and given by \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\) if the charge is outside the surface, and \(\oint_S \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\) if charges of magnitude \(q\) were inside the surface.

answer.text: \(\oint_s \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} \neq 0\) on any surface.
\(\oint_s \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\) if the charge is outside the surface.
\(\oint_s \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) could not be defined.
\(\oint_s \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\) if charges of magnitude \(q\) were inside the surface.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_11 - Electric field outside neutral charge distribution

questiontext.text: 1.11 Consider a region inside which there are various types of charges but the total charge is zero. At points outside the region

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a localized charge distribution with zero net charge (such as an electric dipole or higher multipole), the electric field at a large distance \(r\) can be analyzed using multipole expansion, and any electrostatic field is conservative.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even when the total charge is zero, the electric field outside the region need not be zero (for example, an electric dipole has zero net charge but produces a non-zero electric field). The field is not necessarily due to the dipole moment alone, as higher-order multipoles (like quadrupole moments) may also contribute.
However, since the monopole term (\(\propto \frac{1}{r^2}\)) vanishes when total charge is zero, the leading (dominant) term at large distances \(r\) is the dipole field, which varies as \(\frac{1}{r^3}\).
Additionally, because the electrostatic field is conservative, the line integral \(\oint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = 0\) around any closed path, so the work done in moving a charged particle along a closed path away from the region is zero.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, at points outside the region, the dominant electric field is proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^3}\) for large \(r\), and the work done to move a charged particle along a closed path away from the region will be zero.

answer.text: the electric field is necessarily zero.
the electric field is due to the dipole moment of the charge distribution only.
the dominant electric field is \(\propto \frac{1}{r^3}\), for large \(r\), where \(r\) is the distance from a origin in this region.
the work done to move a charged particle along a closed path, away from the region, will be zero.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_12 - Flux and field on spherical Gaussian surface

questiontext.text:
1.12 Refer to the arrangement of charges in Fig. 1.6 and a Gaussian surface of radius \(R\) with \(Q\) at the centre. Then

Fig. 1.6

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A spherical Gaussian surface of radius \(R\) has a charge \(Q\) at its centre. A charge \(-2Q\) is located inside the sphere at a distance \(\frac{R}{2}\) from the centre, and a charge \(5Q\) is located outside the sphere at a distance \(R\) from the surface (i.e., \(2R\) from the centre).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
We apply Gauss's law to the spherical surface, taking outward flux as positive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Gauss's law, the total electric flux through the closed surface is \(\Phi_E = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The total charge enclosed inside the Gaussian sphere is:
\[q_{\text{enc}} = Q + (-2Q) = -Q\]
Thus, the total electric flux through the surface of the sphere is \(\Phi_E = \frac{-Q}{\varepsilon_0}\).
Because the charge \(5Q\) lies outside the Gaussian surface, its net flux contribution through the closed surface is zero.
The electric field on the surface of the sphere is the vector sum of fields due to \(Q\), \(-2Q\), and \(5Q\). Since \(-2Q\) is off-centre (at distance \(\frac{R}{2}\) from the centre) and \(5Q\) is outside, the distance from \(-2Q\) to different points on the sphere varies, so the field due to \(-2Q\) is not the same everywhere on the surface, nor is the total field equal to \(\frac{-Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the total flux through the surface of the sphere is \(\frac{-Q}{\varepsilon_0}\), and the flux through the surface of the sphere due to \(5Q\) is zero.

field on the surface of the sphere is \(\frac{-Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}\).
flux through the surface of sphere due to \(5Q\) is zero.
field on the surface of sphere due to \(-2Q\) is same everywhere.

name.text: PHYSICS_ELECTRICCHARGESANDFIELDS_MCQII_Q1_13 - Equilibrium of test charge at centre of ring

questiontext.text:
1.13 A positive charge \(Q\) is uniformly distributed along a circular ring of radius \(R\). A small test charge \(q\) is placed at the centre of the ring (Fig. 1.7). Then

Fig. 1.7

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A positive charge \(Q\) is uniformly distributed along a circular ring of radius \(R\), and a small test charge \(q\) is placed at the centre of the ring.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Displacements are considered either within the plane of the ring or along the axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The electrostatic potential at a distance \(z\) along the axis of a uniformly charged ring is \(V(z) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{\sqrt{R^2 + z^2}}\), and the axial electric field is \(E_z = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qz}{(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\). In the plane of the ring near the centre (\(r \ll R\)), the potential increases radially outward from the centre.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. In the plane of the ring: If \(q > 0\) is displaced slightly from the centre towards one side of the ring, it experiences a stronger repulsion from the nearer arc of positive charge than from the farther arc, so it is pushed back towards the centre (stable equilibrium).
2. If \(q < 0\) is displaced from the centre in the plane of the ring, the attraction towards the nearer arc of positive charge exceeds that of the farther arc, so the net force pulls it further away from the centre (unstable equilibrium), and it continues moving until it hits the ring.
3. Along the axis of the ring: For small axial displacement \(z \ll R\), \(E_z \approx \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Qz}{R^3}\). If \(q < 0\), the force is \(F_z = qE_z = -\left(\frac{|q|Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^3}\right)z\). Since \(F_z \propto -z\), it is a restoring force and the charge performs simple harmonic motion (SHM).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Hence, for \(q > 0\) displaced in the plane of the ring, it is pushed back towards the centre; for \(q < 0\) displaced in the plane of the ring, it never returns and continues moving till it hits the ring; and for \(q < 0\) displaced slightly along the axis, it performs SHM.

answer.text: If \(q > 0\) and is displaced away from the centre in the plane of the ring, it will be pushed back towards the centre.
If \(q < 0\) and is displaced away from the centre in the plane of the ring, it will never return to the centre and will continue moving till it hits the ring.
If \(q < 0\), it will perform SHM for small displacement along the axis.
\(q\) at the centre of the ring is in an unstable equilibrium within the plane of the ring for \(q > 0\).
